8.title: the thoughts that aren't you
8.tomorrow: feet on the floor, hands on the knees
8.howItsDone: In many forms of meditation, people let thoughts come and go without following them, often noting them simply as "thinking" and returning to the breath; Stoic practice examines the judgments behind troubling thoughts instead.

segments.voice: Yesterday: karma, and the intention is the seed. Week one is behind you. Week two starts inside your head.

Here's a thought for you: you left the stove on. Did you? Probably not. But for half a second, your stomach believed it. Thoughts arrive like that all day, uninvited, sounding completely sure of themselves. One large study checked in with people through their phones, at random moments, and asked what they were doing and what they were thinking about. Their minds were somewhere else almost half the time. Two words help with that. Not you. Weather.
screen: `YOU LEFT THE STOVE ON.` → `ALMOST HALF THE TIME, ELSEWHERE.` → `NOT YOU. WEATHER.`

segments.voice: In 1890, William James described something everyone lives with and few had put well: the stream of thought. Consciousness, he wrote, "is nothing jointed; it flows." A river, not a row of boxes. Thoughts come and go on it, and you didn't send most of them. Nearly two thousand years earlier, the Greek teacher Epictetus, who was born enslaved, came at it another way. In an old translation: "Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things." The trouble is less the event than the judgment we add on top of it, and that judgment is ours to examine. Many Buddhist teachers, especially in the Tibetan tradition, use a picture you may like: the mind is like the sky, and thoughts are like weather. Clouds, storms, bright spells. They move through. The sky isn't the clouds, and it isn't harmed by them. A stream, an opinion you can question, weather in the sky. Three different pictures, and each one treats a thought as something that happens in you, not the whole of you.
screen: `IT IS NOTHING JOINTED; IT FLOWS.` · `NOT THINGS, BUT OPINIONS.` · `THE SKY AND THE WEATHER.` · `SOMETHING THAT HAPPENS IN YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. The bell gives you about forty-five seconds. Sit, and let the breath settle. When a thought shows up, name it quietly: thinking. Don't follow it, and don't fight it. Watch it move on, the way weather does. Then you're back here, in the body that's breathing.
Thoughts. Things that happen in you, like weather. Not the whole of you. Eighth word.
Your line: let it pass. Not every thought that sounds sure of itself gets a vote. Day eight.

screen: `DAY 8 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: FEET ON THE FLOOR, HANDS ON THE KNEES.`

9.title: feet on the floor, hands on the knees
9.hook: feet on the floor, hands on the knees — you have one
9.howItsDone: Yoga, Zen and many Buddhist and Christian contemplative practices begin by settling the body: a steady, comfortable seat, feet grounded, hands at rest, with attention on how the body feels.

segments.voice: Yesterday: thoughts, and let it pass. Today, the place that sits underneath them.

Quick check. Where are your feet right now? If that took a second to answer, no surprise. A day can be lived about a foot above your own shoulders: in a screen, in a conversation that already happened, in tomorrow's list. Meanwhile there's a whole body down here, keeping you alive, carrying you around, sending messages that mostly go unopened. Feet on the floor. Hands on the knees. You have one.
screen: `WHERE ARE YOUR FEET?` → `A FOOT ABOVE YOUR SHOULDERS.` → `YOU HAVE ONE.`

segments.voice: Start with an old instruction for sitting. The Yoga Sutras, compiled in India and traditionally credited to Patanjali, say almost nothing about the poses people now call yoga. On posture they're very brief: the seat should be steady and easy. The word is asana, and there it means simply a seat, the place you sit. Steady, so you're not fidgeting. Easy, so you're not straining. One of the oldest Buddhist teachings on mindfulness puts the body first too: breathing in, breathing out, standing, walking, sitting, lying down. Knowing, plainly, what the body is doing while it's doing it. Then, in 1890, William James turned common sense around. Common sense says we cry because we're sad. James said it may run the other way: "we feel sorry because we cry, angry because we strike, afraid because we tremble." Psychologists have argued about how far that goes ever since. The smaller point is one you can check for yourself: body and feeling are tangled together, and a change in one tends to show up in the other. That's why the body makes such a good doorway. You can't always choose your thoughts. You can usually choose to put your feet flat on the floor.
screen: `ASANA: A SEAT, STEADY AND EASY.` · `MINDFULNESS STARTS WITH THE BODY.` · `AFRAID BECAUSE WE TREMBLE.` · `FEET FLAT ON THE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Before the bell, set your feet flat on the floor if you can, and rest your hands on your knees or in your lap. For about forty-five seconds, feel three things in turn: your feet, whatever is holding you up, and your hands, just resting. Steady and easy. That's the whole seat.
Body. Where mindfulness starts, and a place you can always come back to. Ninth word.
Your line: come back down. Your feet are always somewhere to land. See you tomorrow.

pairs: a choice you can usually make

10.title: pascal: the quiet room
10.hook: Pascal: all the unhappiness of men arises from one single fact, that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber (Pensées 139, Trotter's 1910 translation)
10.howItsDone: Many traditions have a practice of simply sitting still: Zen Buddhists sit zazen, often facing a wall; Quakers gather in silent worship; and many people keep a few quiet minutes alone at the start or end of the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: body, and come back down. Today, the hardest easy thing there is.

Try this, just in your head. You're in a plain room. No phone. No book. Nobody else. Nothing to do for fifteen minutes. How long before you reach for something? Researchers at the University of Virginia tried a version of this in 2014. They left people alone with nothing but their thoughts and a button that gave a mild electric shock. People who had already tried the shock, and said they'd pay to avoid it, still pushed the button: most of the men, and about a quarter of the women. Anything, rather than just sitting. More than three hundred and fifty years earlier, a French mathematician saw this coming.
screen: `A PLAIN ROOM. NOTHING TO DO.` → `A BUTTON.` → `ANYTHING BUT SITTING.`

segments.voice: His name was Blaise Pascal. As a young man he built one of the first mechanical calculators and did serious work on probability. Later, after an intense religious experience, he filled his last years with notes toward a defense of Christian faith. He died at thirty-nine, and his friends published the notes as the Pensées, the thoughts. You may have seen one on a poster: all of humanity's problems stem from man's inability to sit quietly in a room alone. That's a modern paraphrase. An old English translation has it this way: "I have discovered that all the unhappiness of men arises from one single fact, that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber." Not problems. Unhappiness. And listen to his reason. A man will chase a hare all day, Pascal says, that he wouldn't take if you handed it to him. He doesn't want the hare. He wants the chase, because it keeps him from thinking about himself. Pascal's own answer to what waits in the quiet room was a Christian one. But his observation stands by itself: the restlessness isn't a sign something is wrong with you. He saw it in everyone. Zen Buddhism in Japan built a whole practice around sitting, called zazen. The teacher Dogen taught a form called shikantaza, just sitting: no goal, nothing to win. You sit, and the restlessness comes and goes like anything else. Two very different reasons. Both noticed the chair.
screen: `THE POSTER LINE IS A PARAPHRASE.` · `THE HARE HE WOULDN'T TAKE.` · `ZEN: JUST SITTING.` · `THE RESTLESSNESS IS EVERYONE'S.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. The bell gives you about forty-five seconds. Let your hands rest in your lap. Sit. Breathe. Notice the small pull to do something else. You don't have to fight it, and you don't have to obey it. That pull is exactly what Pascal was writing about, and you're sitting with it.
Sit. The simplest instruction there is, and somehow one of the hardest. Not to do anything. Just to stay. Tenth word.
Your line: sit anyway. A restless sit still counts as a sit, every time. Day ten.

11.title: 144 times a day
11.hook: 144 times a day; putting it face down is a practice
11.howItsDone: Sabbath-observant Jews set phones aside from Friday sundown to Saturday nightfall, and some people of other backgrounds keep a weekly tech sabbath or phone-free meals.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sit, and sit anyway. Today, the thing that makes sitting so hard. It may be in your hand.

A hundred and forty-four. That's how many times a day, according to one survey of Americans, people check their phones. Spread over sixteen waking hours, it's about once every six or seven minutes. And there's a decent chance you're listening to this on one. A lot of those checks don't feel like decisions. The hand just goes. Nobody here is going to tell you to throw it in a lake. It's how you talk to people you love, and it's how you got here today. But today's idea is small and a little radical: putting it face down is a practice.
screen: `ABOUT 144 TIMES A DAY.` → `THE HAND JUST GOES.` → `FACE DOWN IS A PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: Remember Pascal from yesterday, who traced the unhappiness of men to one fact: "they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber"? He was writing about hunting and gambling and the royal court. He never saw a phone. But he'd recognize the reach of the hand. In 2017, researchers at the University of Texas ran a simple experiment. People did tests of attention and memory with their phones either on the desk face down, in a pocket or bag, or in another room. All the phones were silent. The people whose phones were in another room did best. The phone didn't have to buzz. Just being nearby seemed to pull at part of the mind. So face down is a start, and the next room is even better. And an old practice already knows this shape. In Jewish tradition, the Sabbath is a day each week when work stops, from sundown Friday to nightfall Saturday. The rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel described it as a kind of palace built in time rather than in space: not a place you go, but a stretch of hours you protect. For Sabbath-observant Jews, the phone is set down with the rest of the week's work. Some people outside Judaism now keep what they call a tech sabbath. You don't have to start with a whole day. The point isn't that the phone is bad. The point is that the hand should be yours.
screen: `PASCAL NEVER SAW A PHONE.` · `ANOTHER ROOM DID BEST.` · `A PALACE BUILT IN TIME.` · `THE HAND SHOULD BE YOURS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. If you're not listening on your phone, put it face down now, or in a bag. If you are, set it down, screen down, as the bell starts. Then sit for about forty-five seconds. Notice any pull toward it: the hand, the itch, the thought that something might be waiting. Just notice the pull, and let it pass, like weather. It'll still be there after the bell.
The phone. A tool you love, and a hand that reaches on its own, until you put it face down on purpose. Eleventh word.
Your line: face down for three minutes. Three minutes is enough to find out whose hand it is. That's day eleven.

screen: `DAY 11 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE QUIET THE MYSTICS SHARE.`

12.title: the quiet the mystics share
12.hook: mystics disagree about almost everything; they all got quiet
12.tomorrow: the Tao: those who know they have enough are rich
12.howItsDone: Silence is practiced in many forms: Quaker meetings for worship held in shared silence, silent retreats in Christian and Buddhist monasteries, and the Orthodox practice of stillness called hesychasm.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the phone, face down for three minutes. Today, what's left when the noise stops.

When was the last time you heard nothing? Not quiet with a podcast. Not quiet with the fridge humming and a phone buzzing in the next room. Nothing. It's easy to go a long time without it. The car, the shower, the walk to the store all get filled. Here's something odd. The mystics of the world's traditions disagree about a great deal: God, the soul, what happens after death. But read what they actually did, and one thing keeps showing up, from monasteries to meeting houses to mountain caves. They got quiet.
screen: `WHEN DID YOU LAST HEAR NOTHING?` → `THEY DISAGREE ABOUT A LOT.` → `AND THEY GOT QUIET.`

segments.voice: Start with a prophet on the run. Elijah hides in a cave on a mountain. A great wind comes, tearing rocks apart, but God is not in the wind. Then an earthquake, and God is not in the earthquake. Then fire, and God is not in the fire. And then, in the King James wording, "after the fire a still small voice." That Hebrew phrase is hard to carry into English; it has also been rendered a gentle whisper, and a sound of thin silence. Either way, what comes after the noise is quiet. Eastern Orthodox monks on Mount Athos in Greece are known for a way of prayer called hesychasm, from a Greek word meaning stillness. In traditional Quaker meetings, Friends worship by sitting together in silence, speaking only when someone feels moved to. Early Buddhist texts describe the Buddha telling monks that when they gather, they should either talk about the teaching or keep what he called noble silence. And an old Chinese classic puts it sharply: those who know don't talk about it, and those who talk about it don't know. These traditions don't agree about what's found in the silence. For some it's God; for some, the mind seeing itself clearly; for some, the Tao, which can't be named. But it's a room each of them walks into. For each, in its own way, quiet is where it is.
screen: `NOT THE WIND, NOT THE FIRE.` · `STILLNESS, MEETING, NOBLE SILENCE.` · `THOSE WHO KNOW DON'T TALK.` · `DIFFERENT THINGS, THE SAME ROOM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. If you can, turn off one sound near you: the music, the TV, the notifications. Then sit. For the next forty-five seconds, don't try to make the mind silent. Just listen to the silence that's already around the sounds. The hum, and the space around the hum. If you pray, you can hold a line from the Psalms: be still, and know. If you don't, just listen.
Silence. A room that prophets, monks, Friends and sages all walk into, even when they find different things there. Twelfth word.
Your line: quiet is where it is. A stretch you don't fill can be a room of its own. That's day twelve.

screen: `DAY 12 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE TAO: THOSE WHO KNOW THEY HAVE ENOUGH ARE RICH.`

13.title: the Tao: those who know they have enough are rich
13.hook: the Tao: those who know they have enough are rich
13.howItsDone: Contentment is practiced on several paths: Taoists speak of knowing enough, Stoics and Epicureans practiced living simply, and some people keep a habit of pausing to name what they already have.

segments.voice: Yesterday: silence, and quiet is where it is. Today, a word that's surprisingly hard to say about your own life.

The shoes arrive. Or the phone, or the upgrade. For a few days there's a glow. Then, often, it's just a thing that's owned, and the wanting has already moved on to the next one. Kurt Vonnegut told a story about this. He and his fellow novelist Joseph Heller were at a party given by a billionaire. Vonnegut pointed out that their host might have made more in a single day than Heller's best-known novel had earned in its whole life. Heller said he had something the billionaire could never have: the knowledge that he had enough.
screen: `THE GLOW, THEN THE NEXT THING.` → `A PARTY GIVEN BY A BILLIONAIRE.` → `SOMETHING HE CAN NEVER HAVE.`

segments.voice: Heller was in old company. The Tao Te Ching, the short Chinese classic traditionally credited to Lao-tzu, has a chapter of paired sayings about strength and knowledge. In the middle of it, in an old translation: "He who is satisfied with his lot is rich." In the Chinese it's four characters, and the first two mean knowing enough. Not having enough. Knowing it. Richness, in this picture, isn't a number in a bank account. It's a kind of recognition. The Roman Stoic Seneca made the same turn in a letter to a friend: the poor person isn't the one who has too little, but the one who keeps craving more. And the Greek philosopher Epicurus, whose name now gets attached to fine dining, is reported to have been content with bread and water, and to have prized friendship above almost anything. Modern psychologists have a name for what all three were pushing against: the hedonic treadmill. When we get something we wanted, we get used to it, fast, and our sense of normal moves up. So the chase never finishes, because the finish line walks away as we approach it. Knowing enough doesn't mean you stop wanting anything or never improve your life. It means that now and then you step off the treadmill and say the word. The traditions that teach it don't promise it'll make you rich. They say it's what rich actually is.
screen: `SATISFIED WITH HIS LOT IS RICH.` · `THE POOR ONE KEEPS CRAVING MORE.` · `THE HEDONIC TREADMILL.` · `STEP OFF, AND SAY THE WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let the breath settle. For about forty-five seconds, let your eyes or your mind move over what you have right now. Not the whole house, just what's in reach. The chair holding you up. The clothes you're wearing. The breath coming in without being asked. For each one, say inside: enough. Not forever. Just, right now, enough.
Enough. Not having it: knowing it. The quiet partner to every vision board. Thirteenth word.
Your line: enough. The one thing in the story the billionaire couldn't buy. Day thirteen.

screen: `DAY 13 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THREE THINGS, OUT LOUD, BADLY.`

14.title: three things, out loud, badly
14.tomorrow: the rule that keeps turning up
14.howItsDone: Many people keep a short gratitude practice: a few things written in a notebook each night, a thanksgiving said at meals, or, in Jewish tradition, a brief prayer of thanks said on waking.

segments.voice: Yesterday: enough, and knowing it. Today closes week two, with three things, said badly.

Family dinner. Somebody says, okay, everyone name one thing you're thankful for. Half the table groans. Somebody says the food. Somebody says Wi-Fi. A kid says the dog. It's awkward, it's a bit forced, and it's over in a minute. That clumsy minute may be worth more than it looks. Today asks for three things. Out loud. Badly. Not eloquent, not the perfect list. Just said.
screen: `NAME ONE THING.` → `THE FOOD, THE WI-FI, THE DOG.` → `THREE THINGS, OUT LOUD, BADLY.`

segments.voice: Start with the emperor from day three. Marcus Aurelius's private notebook doesn't open with philosophy at all, at least as it comes down to us. It opens with a list of thank-yous. From his grandfather, good morals and an even temper. From his mother, generosity, and a simple way of living. Teacher after teacher, friend after friend, what each one gave him. A man who ruled an empire starts by counting what he'd been given. Paul, writing to a young church, tells them, in old English wording: "In every thing give thanks." Notice he doesn't say for everything. In everything. Inside whatever is happening, find something to thank. Jewish tradition has a short prayer, the Modeh Ani, said on waking, while still in bed, thanking God for giving back the soul for another day. Thanks comes first, before coffee, before news. And then the lab. In 2003 the psychologists Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough asked some people to write down, each week, a few things they were grateful for, while others wrote about hassles or ordinary events. After ten weeks, the gratitude group rated their lives as a whole more highly and felt more hopeful about the week ahead. Nobody was asked to feel grateful first. They were only asked to write it down. That's why badly is allowed. Gratitude isn't a mood you wait for. It's a thing you say, and on hard days you say it anyway. The Stoic Seneca kept an evening version: once the lamp was out, he went back over his day. So if you keep a journal and wonder what to write, here's a pair. In the morning: what matters today? At night: what went well, and what would I do differently?
screen: `AN EMPEROR'S LIST OF THANK-YOUS.` · `IN EVERY THING GIVE THANKS.` · `THANKS BEFORE GETTING OUT OF BED.` · `WRITE IT DOWN, NO FEELING REQUIRED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, and yes, it's out loud. If you're somewhere you can't speak, whisper it, or just move your lips. Name three things you're thankful for right now, the first three that come. They can be tiny: warm socks, a text from someone, the bus that came. Say them badly. Then, for about forty-five seconds, sit with the third one and let it land.
Gratitude. Noticing what you've been given, and saying so, even before the feeling arrives. Fourteenth word. Thoughts, body, sit, the phone, silence, enough, gratitude: that's week two.
Your line: thank you anyway. It matters most on the days it's hardest to say. Day fourteen, done.
